Happy Mylochromis anaphyrmus is a cichlid from Lake Malawi that attains a maximum total length of 20.4 centimeters [Li = 20.4 centimeters], placing it among the medium-sized members of its genus. Field surveys conducted across the southern portion of the lake indicate that individuals typically achieve this asymptotic size after several years of sustained growth in the warm, well-oxygenated littoral environments they inhabit. The species displays a moderately elongated body form characteristic of benthic foraging, with adult specimens commonly encountered over sandy substrates interspersed with rocks. Growth rates in natural populations appear to be density-dependent, with fish from less crowded habitats reaching larger sizes more consistently. Comparative data from congeners such as Mylochromis lateristriga suggest that the maximum length of Happy is broadly typical for the genus, although some species in the group can exceed 25 centimeters. The ultimate body size of this species likely reflects selective pressures associated with its diet of benthic invertebrates and small crustaceans, which requires maneuverability rather than extreme bulk. Long-term monitoring of marked individuals in protected areas confirms that the species maintains a stable adult size distribution across years with variable food availability.

Reproductive maturation in Happy occurs at a total length of 14 centimeters [Lp = 14 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds with the onset of gonadal development in both sexes. Examination of preserved museum specimens reveals that individuals below this length consistently possess immature gonads, while those above it show clear evidence of vitellogenesis or spermatogenesis. The length at puberty represents approximately 69 percent of the ultimate length, a proportion that is intermediate among Lake Malawi cichlids and suggests a life-history strategy that balances early reproduction with continued growth. Field observations indicate that males and females reach this size at roughly the same age, although some variation exists across populations from different parts of the lake. The attainment of puberty in this species is likely influenced by social factors, as dominant individuals in hierarchical groups may mature earlier than subordinates even when body sizes are comparable. Seasonal patterns in water temperature and prey abundance also modulate the timing of gonadal recrudescence, with spawning activity peaking during the warm, stable months when food resources are most plentiful for developing offspring.

The wet weight at birth for Happy has been estimated at 0.0011 grams [Wwb = 0.0011 grams], reflecting the small size of the fertilised ovum from which the yolk-sac larva emerges. This minute initial mass is derived from the dimensions of the pelagic eggs, which are typical of cichlids that practice maternal mouthbrooding and produce numerous small offspring rather than a few large ones. Newly hatched larvae remain entirely endotrophic during the first several days post-eclosion, relying on endogenous yolk reserves before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The low birth weight imposes a high initial mortality risk, as the tiny prolarvae are vulnerable to predation and environmental fluctuations during the critical period before their mouth gape opens and first prey capture becomes possible. Despite the small size of individual neonates, the overall reproductive investment can be substantial because females may produce several hundred eggs per spawning event. The ratio of birth weight to adult female weight is among the lowest recorded for Malawi cichlids, consistent with a bet-hedging strategy that spreads reproductive effort across many small offspring rather than concentrating it in a few well-provisioned young. This early life stage is particularly sensitive to the availability of microscopic plankton, and survival during the first weeks after yolk-sac resorption largely determines recruitment success in natural populations.

Adults of this species achieve a maximum wet weight of 120 grams [Wwi = 120 grams], a figure that aligns closely with predictions from length-weight regressions developed for other members of the haplochromine group. This asymptotic body mass is attained when individuals reach their ultimate total length and reflects the accumulation of somatic tissues and energy reserves necessary for sustaining reproductive output over multiple breeding seasons. The body condition of adult Happy fluctuates seasonally, with peak masses recorded just before the main spawning period when females are gravid and males have well-developed fat stores. Comparative data from other benthic-feeding cichlids in Lake Malawi indicate that a maximum mass of approximately 120 grams is typical for species occupying similar trophic niches and attaining comparable adult lengths. The weight-length relationship in this species follows the general pattern observed across the genus, with females tending to be slightly heavier than males of the same length when in reproductive condition. Long-term ecological studies suggest that food availability in the rocky-littoral zone supports consistent attainment of this maximum mass across most years, although drought-related reductions in lake level can temporarily depress body condition.

At the onset of reproductive maturity, Happy individuals typically weigh approximately 39.3 grams [Wwp = approximately 39.3 grams], representing roughly one-third of the ultimate adult mass. This weight at puberty indicates that substantial growth continues after the initiation of breeding activity, allowing individuals to increase their reproductive potential as they age and grow larger. The energetic demands of gamete production at this body size are considerable, as females must allocate resources to vitellogenesis while simultaneously supporting their own maintenance requirements. Field data collected from trawl samples indicate that first-time spawners at this weight produce smaller clutches than older, heavier females, a pattern consistent with the general relationship between maternal size and fecundity observed across oviparous fishes. The species exhibits iteroparous reproduction, with mature individuals spawning repeatedly across multiple seasons under favorable conditions. These fish experience a maximum lifespan of 6 years [am = 6 years] when maintained at a stable water temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C], allowing for multiple reproductive cycles and contributing to the species' persistence in the variable littoral environment. Older individuals show signs of reproductive senescence, with declining fecundity and gamete quality evident in the oldest age classes.
